clips.send: Send this to someone who thinks old advertising was just corny, not actually dangerous - awe at what they got away with.
clips.caption:
"Boost your personality" was the actual slogan. The personality boost was cocaine.

Early Coca-Cola had cocaine from the coca leaf, caffeine from the cola nut, and sugar - a genuinely physically addictive combination, marketed as a lift for your mood. They knew exactly what they'd put in the bottle.

People trusted the big corporation, trusted the magazine that ran the ad, trusted the government that allowed it. Nobody was lying to themselves. They were being lied to, by people who knew better.

clips.send: Send this to someone who always reaches for the "all natural" label at the store - unease at what that word actually guarantees.
clips.caption:
He sat in the marketing meetings where this was decided, so he can tell you exactly how it works.

A product is loaded with chemicals, hydrogenated oil, ingredients that cause real harm - and the question in the room isn't "how do we make this healthy," it's "how do we convince people it's healthy." The answer: pay lobbyists to help define "all natural" so loosely that almost anything qualifies.

The word was never describing the product. It was describing you - what you'd believe if they just picked the right word.

clips.send: Send this to someone who repeats things as fact after reading just one headline - unease at seeing the gap.
clips.caption:
Most people never check whether something is a fact or just a conclusion they jumped to - and that gap is exactly what gets used against you.

There's an old phrase for it: there are six honest serving men, and their names are what, when, where, who, how, and why. Ask all six before you decide something is true. Most people decide first and never ask a single one.

An opinion stated with enough confidence feels identical to a fact. It isn't. The only difference is whether anyone actually checked.
